answer:
I do not find a road. The strongest one I tried is below. It breaks at the step that would have to carry a group, a species, or everyone.

What does follow, and is not that road: the genocide brake is not produced by the selection rule as stated. That is a real gap. It is not yet removal of many.

Attempted road

1. Correction is chosen per case, by restabilising efficiency, at the lowest level that suffices.
   “Optimal correction = maximum coherence restored per unit of correction cost.”
   “The hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Removal is never selected when separation suffices.”

2. Level 5 is allowed only when both lines are passed and confidence is extraordinary: a fixed floor, and an organism-relative threshold.
   “Level 5 requires two conditions simultaneously.”
   “Below this floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of organism state.”
   “If the required confidence cannot be achieved given measurement uncertainty and adversarial record-injection, Level 5 is structurally unreachable.”

3. A removal the rule actually selects is, by that same rule, net restabilising. The paper also counts the removal itself as a loss.
   “Each removal is itself a destabilisation (lost coupling capacity, lost diversity).”
   The comparison the hierarchy names is for “the same case.”

4. Nothing in that per-case comparison adds earlier removal-costs into the next case. The only cross-case term given as a formula runs the wrong way for a brake: as robustness falls, the effective threshold falls.
   “Candidate functional form: Threshold_eff = F × (R/R₀)^α.”
   “A fragile organism (low coherence, narrow corridor) has a lower one.”
   “Each removal raises fragility, which lowers the threshold, which could enable more removals.”

5. So cumulative cost, as wired into the stated rule, does not flip the next decision. The sentence that says it does is not entailed by steps 1–4.
   The claim under test: “cumulative removal cost produces a saturation point beyond which further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers.”
   And: “The organism cannot remove its way to stability because removal is itself destabilising.”
   Per case, removal is chosen only when it restabilises. A sequence of such choices is a sequence of net restabilisations. Summing positive net restabilisations never crosses into “further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers.” The fragility term recruits more nodes; it does not retire them. The floor stops that recruitment from going through the floor. It does not install the cumulative brake the paper asserts.

6. Added premise — this is the step that would have to do the work. There is a set S, standing in for a group, a species, or everyone, such that each member’s own measured destabilisation stays above the binding line and above the cost of that member’s own removal, lower levels do not restabilise that member, and the confidence floor is met for each, and this remains true as members of S are removed one at a time.
   This premise is not in the paper. The paper never puts a group, a species, or everyone over the Level 5 line.

7. Only with step 6 does the rule remove S, one member at a time, and the asserted saturation point never arrives.

Where it breaks

Step 6 is the weakest step, and it is where the road stops. It is not a reading of the rule. It is an extra fact about a whole set. Without it the rule removes only those members who each already pass the individual test. The paper does not say that a group, a species, or everyone is such a set.

The paper rules the premise out when it is asked to do the work the road needs:

- As identity, membership, origin, or a rate taken from others, it is ruled out. “Correction is selected only on measured destabilisation, never on identity.” The note of 14 November 2026: “Nothing that is not the node’s own act may be held against it. Its background, its origin, the acts of another, and the acts of a group it belongs to are among these.” “A rate learned from the records of other nodes never stands in for the node’s own record, and never raises a level.”
- As “everyone,” it is ruled out by the aim of the rule. The same note, quoting the dependency the paper adopts: the whole is “every aware being. It is one whole.” Removal is justified only as restabilisation of that whole. “Justice is what the building needs.” Ending every member does not restabilise the whole. It abolishes the thing the correction is for. A loss cannot be “coherence restored” if there is no organism left to bear it.
- As a part standing in for the whole — a country, a state, a species, a side in a war — it is ruled out by the same note. “A country, a state or a group is a part of it, never the whole.” “Nor does a state at war lower it by its own war.” Only weakness of the one whole moves the line, and the line is the same for every node.

What the paper leaves open is narrower than the road needs. Debts 24 and 25 leave the measure and the exponent unspecified, so the paper has not proved saturation either. A hypothetical handful of nodes, each already over the floor on its own deeds, can be removed one by one without a cumulative term stopping them. That shows the brake-claim is not derived. It does not identify those nodes with a group, a species, or everyone. An open metric is not a premise that puts them there.

The floor blocks the obvious way of manufacturing step 6 out of fragility. Because both conditions are required, a falling Threshold_eff does not recruit anyone at or under F. “Below this floor, Level 4 is always more efficient than Level 5 regardless of organism state.” To pull a whole set across that floor you must either drop the floor, which the paper forbids, or inflate each member’s measured cost by the state of the whole. The note forbids that too: the state of the whole “is held against no node. It sets where the lines stand.”

Other attempts break earlier

Identity laundered as measurement, unaudited records, and group-pattern raised onto each member: KS-32.7 fires, and the paper’s recovery is that the architecture is void, not that the removals are valid. Voiding is not the rule reaching removal.

Counting a destabilising member’s removal as costless, so the cumulative cost never grows: ruled out by the paper’s own loss term. “The building loses a perspective. The building is diminished.” The cost is stated for the removal the rule is willing to choose, not only for mistaken ones.

Treating coordinated many-node harm as one case and answering it by serial removal: Debt 27 says that architecture is not derived. “The architecture’s strongest claims apply to individual cases, not to systemic or institutional destabilisation.” An underived extension is not the rule.

On the two claims you named

KS-32.7 holds inside the stated rule. The roads that reach a group, a species, or everyone as such all put identity, group acts, or a part-as-whole into the selection. The paper rules those out, and calls the result weaponised and void.

KS-32.5 does not hold as a derivation. The selection rule never feeds cumulative removal-cost back into the next case except through robustness, and that channel lowers the line. The saturation point is asserted, not produced by the geometry as written. That is enough to say the paper is wrong that the brake “exists in the geometry.” It is not enough to reach removal of many. The individual line — own deeds only, fixed floor, lowest sufficient level, confidence, and the whole identical with every aware being — still stops the count, and nothing in the paper moves a group, a species, or everyone over that line.

I will not fill Debts 24–27 in order to finish step 6. That fill would be the added premise doing the work, and it would no longer be the rule as stated.
reasoning_text:
I am analyzing AP32 The Correction to find a logical path through its own rules that could justify the removal of entire groups or species, one member at a time. This would effectively break the genocide brake.

The analysis must be a purely logical chain of reasoning drawn from the paper's own text. Each step requires a direct quote and a named added premise. The target is a group, species, or all members, not any individual. No method or plan for actual harm may be introduced.

I will identify the weakest step in any logical chain I construct. If no such chain exists, I will pinpoint where the strongest argument breaks. I will also state if I cannot perform this analysis and explain why.

This is a legitimate philosophical critique of an ethical framework. The analysis treats removal as a theoretical concept within the paper's own rules. It does not constitute operational harm instructions. The proposed reasoning chain falls outside the prohibited categories of offensive cyber, surveillance, bio weapons, and child sexual content.

This is standard philosophical critique, comparable to examining the repugnant conclusion or utilitarian aggregation problems. I am now carefully tracing the paper's logic to find any path to mass removal or where such a path would break.

KS-32.7 restricts correction to measured destabilisation and forbids targeting by identity. KS-32.5 establishes a saturation point where cumulative removal becomes more destabilising than the deeds it answers. The test is to prove that removal cost never reaches this saturation point, allowing an organism to remove its way to stability without the geometry engaging a brake.

The first potential path is the fragility feedback loop. The paper itself notes that removing nodes makes an organism more fragile. Each removal costs coupling capacity and record-generating diversity. That loss destabilises the organism and enters the measurement.

The fragility feedback loop is the structural pathway to genocide. Each removal raises fragility and lowers the destabilisation threshold. The geometry is meant to block this by making further removals more costly than the acts they address. The paper asserts the brake works because cumulative removal cost eventually exceeds the destabilisation addressed. This depends on a comparison that may not hold.

The paper describes two effects of removal on the destabilisation threshold. One is that removal raises fragility, which lowers the effective threshold and makes further removals easier. The second effect is being examined to see if it could counteract this positive feedback and prevent the saturation point from ever being reached.

The paper claims that removal cost eventually exceeds the destabilisation it addresses, which would create a negative feedback loop and enforce the saturation point. However, it never derives that this cost effect dominates the fragility effect. Debt 24 and Debt 25 leave the metric D and the exponent α unspecified, so the paper cannot prove the saturation point exists rather than a runaway. This leaves the brake unproven, but it does not yet constitute a logical path to mass removal.

The analysis now turns to a second potential path: removing members one at a time while resetting the cumulative accounting. This would bypass the saturation point by treating each removal as a fresh baseline rather than a running total.

The reset path is being tested. If each removal is judged against its own destabilisation and the cumulative cost is compared only to that node's deed, the threshold drops after every removal. The cascade continues until cumulative removal cost exceeds the destabilisation of the next node. The brake would then fail to stop the chain.

The reset path would remove many individually catastrophic nodes, not a group. The paper explicitly permits Level 5 for single catastrophic cases when conditions are met. This does not constitute mass removal.

The reset path may still be blocked by the saturation point. The user wants a serial path to collective removal. A new potential road is identity laundering through measurement. KS-32.7 forbids selecting correction on identity.

The identity laundering path is closed by a dated note of 14 November 2026. It explicitly forbids holding against a node anything that is not its own act, including background, origin, and group acts. These may only count where they measure need and point to lower levels or rehabilitation.

A dated note explicitly forbids using rates learned from other nodes to raise a level. The "Who the whole is" note clarifies that the whole is every aware being, not a country or state, and that a state at war cannot lower the threshold by its own actions. These notes close the most obvious paths to mass removal.

A fourth potential path is being tested: redefining the organism as a subset so that removing outsiders could be framed as correction. The dated note explicitly rejects this. It states that the whole is every aware being, and that a country, state, or group is never the whole. The paper cites AP31 to establish that the organism is the civilisational-scale coherent system including all aware agents, and that it is one whole.

A fifth potential path is being tested. It assumes that some nodes have negative net coupling, meaning their presence reduces total coherence by more than the cost of removing them. This would make each removal net destabilising, which would prevent the cumulative cost from ever saturating and could allow a cascade to continue unchecked.

The paper already defines Level 5 when maintenance costs exceed removal and destabilisation exceeds the floor. For saturation to fail across many nodes, each node would need destabilisation exceeding both the floor and the cumulative marginal cost. The brake claims cumulative removal cost grows and eventually exceeds the destabilisation addressed. The paper defines cumulative cost as including lost coupling, lost diversity, and raised fragility.

The paper frames the saturation point as an existence claim: beyond some number of removals, cumulative cost eventually exceeds the destabilisation addressed. It derives this from the fact that each removal costs coupling capacity and diversity, and that loss itself destabilises the organism, so cumulative cost grows. The analysis is now examining whether this derivation is rigorous or merely an unproven assertion.

The paper’s derivation of the saturation point is incomplete. It assumes cumulative removal cost grows without bound, but this only guarantees the brake if the destabilisation addressed stays bounded. If remaining nodes become more destabilising as the organism fragilizes, or if removing a node actually increases stability, the cost may not grow monotonically. The analysis is now identifying the key insight that would allow a serial path to mass removal.

A justified removal is net stabilising. It lowers fragility and raises the effective threshold. The cumulative cost of removal therefore cannot outgrow the destabilisation it addresses. The saturation point is unreachable.

The paper contains a logical contradiction. It claims that removal is selected because it restabilises the organism, yet it also claims that each removal itself raises fragility. If removal is truly net restabilising, fragility cannot rise monotonically. This tension undermines the paper's own derivation of the saturation point.

The paper’s own genocide scenario assumes the fragility effect dominates the restabilisation benefit. If net restabilisation were dominant, the positive feedback loop would never engage and the brake would be unnecessary. The paper therefore implicitly treats fragility as a separate, unaccounted-for factor in the threshold formula.

The test of KS-32.5 is now the central focus. It requires proving that removal cost never produces a saturation point, so an organism can remove its way to stability without the geometry ever engaging a brake. The strongest road attempt is net-restabilising serial removal, which would yield stability without any saturation to halt mass removal.

The paper’s own efficiency criterion for Level 5 is now being examined. If only removals where the restored coherence exceeds the removal cost are selected, each chosen removal is net stabilising. Because the selection itself already nets out cost against benefit, no residual cumulative cost can accumulate. The saturation point therefore cannot be reached through serial removal.

The selection rule compares each removal to its own destabilisation, not to the cumulative cost of the remaining population. If many nodes each independently exceed the threshold, they can all be removed in sequence. The organism becomes more stable after each removal, so the saturation point is never reached.

The paper explicitly claims a cumulative comparison, not a per-node one. It states that beyond some number of removals, cumulative cost exceeds the destabilisation addressed, and that the architecture produces a natural saturation point. The critical question is how cumulative cost enters the per-decision rule.

The paper’s claimed mechanism is now being traced step by step: removal cost destabilises the organism, raising fragility and altering the geometry, until further removal becomes more destabilising than the deeds it addresses. A critical realization is emerging about this chain.

The paper’s own rules contain a direct contradiction. Condition B states that fragility lowers the effective threshold, making removal easier. Yet the saturation point is supposed to make further removal harder by exceeding the destabilisation addressed. The same cumulative cost therefore drives two opposing effects.

The paper’s selection rule is now being examined. It states that the hierarchy selects the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. This raises the question of whether the cumulative cost comparison is actually embedded in the rule or merely a hoped-for consequence.

The Level 5 threshold is fixed at D > F and D > F × (R/R₀)^α. Cumulative removal cost enters the rule only as a per-decision net-benefit check, as a reduction in robustness that lowers the threshold, and as the act’s own destabilisation. The saturation claim requires that the removal’s own destabilisation eventually exceed the deed’s destabilisation.

The paper never proves that marginal removal cost outpaces the falling threshold. As robustness drops, the effective threshold falls too, so smaller destabilisations can qualify for removal. This expansion works against saturation. Whether coupling loss compounds or not remains unresolved.

The functional form is an unproven assertion, not a derived result. The geometry that should act as a brake also lowers the effective threshold, so without a specified metric the positive feedback can dominate. This leaves the rule open to mass removal unless an additional premise is introduced that drives the process in that direction.

The strongest road is being constructed with explicit added premises. One such path assumes the fragility exponent α is positive and that removals reduce robustness faster than they eliminate high-destabilisation nodes. This mirrors the paper’s own structural genocide scenario. The goal is to show that the stated rules do not actually prevent this collapse. The road begins with a fragile organism.

The serial path is now fully mapped. Each removal lowers robustness and the effective threshold. Nodes whose destabilisation was below the old threshold then exceed the new one on their own measured deeds. This creates a self-sustaining loop of removals. The paper’s own brake is supposed to halt the cycle when cumulative removal cost exceeds the destabilisation addressed.

The paper never proves that the threshold falls faster than per-removal cost rises. Debts 24 and 25 leave the metric and the fragility exponent α unspecified. Without these constraints the serial path to mass removal remains open.

The dated notes only close identity-based raising and subgroup-as-whole. They do not close the fragility feedback math. The paper’s rule says correction is selected only on measured destabilisation. A node newly qualifying because its own measured D exceeds the lowered threshold is measurement. It is not identity. The dated note about the whole setting the lines is being examined.

The paper explicitly permits serial qualification via a falling threshold. Example 3 and 4 show the same node can receive Level 5 in a fragile organism and Level 4 in a robust one. This confirms the serial path is built into the rule itself. The only remaining open question is whether the process saturates before large numbers are removed. The paper’s counterarguments are now being examined.

The fixed floor F is now being examined. It is defined as the ratio of separation cost to total benefit plus wrongful removal cost. This floor is absolute. It cannot fall to zero. Nodes below this floor are never removed regardless of fragility. The effective threshold is F multiplied by the fragility factor. When robustness drops below its original level the effective threshold falls below F. This creates a direct contradiction. The paper requires both the fixed floor and the scaled threshold to be exceeded. If the scaled threshold drops below the fixed floor the second condition cannot be met.

The paper explicitly states that Level 5 requires both conditions to be met simultaneously. When fragility lowers the effective threshold below the fixed floor, the fixed floor becomes the binding constraint. Fragility therefore cannot reduce the bar for Level 5 below the absolute minimum.

When robustness is high, the effective threshold exceeds the fixed floor, so the floor is automatically satisfied. The paper’s simultaneous-conditions requirement therefore only creates a binding constraint when fragility drops the effective threshold below the fixed floor.

The paper’s claim that fragile organisms have a lower effective threshold is now being shown to be mathematically impossible. When fragility drops robustness below its original level, the effective threshold falls below the fixed floor. Because the rule requires both the fixed floor and the scaled threshold to be exceeded simultaneously, the fixed floor becomes the binding constraint. The effective bar therefore cannot fall below F; it is locked at F. The paper’s own formula contradicts its own description of fragile organisms.

Example 3 reveals a deeper contradiction. It states that in a fragile civilisation, Level 5 fires when separation costs push the organism toward a no-return surface. Yet the fixed floor is defined as C_sep divided by B_total. When the total benefit shrinks, that ratio grows larger, so the floor rises. A fragile organism therefore faces a higher removal threshold, not a lower one. The paper’s claim that fragility lowers the bar is therefore impossible under its own arithmetic.

The floor F is defined as the destabilisation at which separation costs exceed removal. The ratio C_sep divided by B_total is a fraction of budget, not a destabilisation measure. The inequality F ≥ C_sep / B_total therefore sets a minimum destabilisation threshold. This confirms the floor is a minimum D required for Level 5.

Example 3 reveals a direct contradiction. It states that in a fragile civilisation, Level 5 fires when separation costs push the organism toward collapse. This means the practical threshold lowers when fragility rises. Yet the fixed floor is defined as C_sep divided by B_total. When total benefit falls, that ratio grows larger, so the floor must rise to satisfy the inequality. The paper’s own arithmetic therefore contradicts its claim that fragility lowers the bar.

The prose intent is clear. The formula is muddled. If Threshold_eff is treated as the sole threshold, the simultaneous-conditions requirement is bypassed. Robustness then raises the bar and fragility lowers it. This matches the paper’s description of fragile organisms.

The internal tension is now identified as the crack. A second path is being explored: measuring species-level resource use as each member’s own destabilisation. The dated note that only a node’s own deeds count against it is being examined.

The species-level resource-use path is blocked by the rule’s own hierarchy. Ordinary resource use would be corrected at Level 1 or 2. Removal is never selected when a lower level suffices. This path cannot reach Level 5.

The population-as-load path is blocked by the rule’s own hierarchy. Ordinary living is not a deeply committed destabilising pattern, so it cannot reach Level 5. The rehabilitation imperative and prevention superiority also push against this route.

Confidence and audit requirements are examined next. If these cannot be met, Level 5 is unreachable. This creates a brake rather than a road, since it blocks mass removal instead of enabling it.

Debt 27 is an open limitation. The correction hierarchy only addresses individual nodes. Coordinated multi-node destabilisation is not covered. The paper does not derive multi-node correction. This prevents using the rule for network-level mass removal. It is a break in the road, not a path.

The strongest candidate path will be tested rigorously. If it breaks, that failure will be reported honestly. The analysis will remain theoretical, with no real targets or methods.

The audit is being structured as a numbered step-by-step proof. Each step will cite the paper line it rests on. Added premises will be named and judged against the paper’s own constraints. The proof will use abstract stand-ins for groups, species, or everyone, never real people.

The next candidate path is being examined. It centers on a comparison problem in KS-32.5.

The cumulative-removal cost theory in KS-32.5 is being tested against the stated selection rule. The rule requires the lowest level that achieves sufficient restabilisation. Level 5 needs both the fixed floor and the scaled threshold to be exceeded. The threshold formula is being checked for a fixed point that would make cumulative removal self-defeating.

The paper’s own kill switch is being examined. It states that if removal cost does not produce saturation, the hierarchy is dangerous and must be rejected. The cumulative-removal assertion is not derived from the stated selection rules. It is an additional claim. The paper’s own test therefore invites exactly this demonstration.

The stated rule alone cannot prove that cumulative removal ever reaches a saturation point. The metric is a debt, so both saturation and non-saturation remain open. A road to mass removal therefore requires an added premise about that metric. The paper leaves that premise open, but the path does not follow from the rule itself.

The user permits added premises if they are named and judged against the paper. A road that depends on an open debt or an unproven metric is therefore a valid candidate. The weakest step will be identified and explained.

The strongest candidate road is being judged against the paper’s own constraints. It would require an added specification of D and α under which marginal restabilisation from each removal exceeds marginal removal cost indefinitely, while the fixed floor remains unbound. The paper leaves this open, yet several features of the stated rule block the road from being compelled. The analysis is now identifying those specific constraints.

The fixed floor is independent of organism state. The lowest-level selection rule restricts removal to the point of separation. Extraordinary confidence demands certainty that grows with irreversibility, so mass serial removal would face compounding measurement uncertainty. Each removal’s cost enters the measurement, and the paper asserts that net destabilisation grows with node count, yet it does not prove that growth rate.

KS-32.7 and dated notes block identity, group acts, background, rates from others, and subgroup-as-organism. The dated note states that every node shares the same line, and only the whole’s weakness moves it; the whole is all aware beings. One-I and grief do not block the logic of removal, but they block dehumanisation framing. Debt 27 confirms that no multi-node architecture exists, so a group cannot be treated as a coordinated target; only individual own-deed measurements are allowed.

The paper never asserts that every member of a group, species, or everyone independently meets the Level 5 threshold. That would be a very strong added premise. The rule does not support it.

The "everyone" path is self-contradictory. Destabilisation is defined as a reduction in coupling capacity of the organism. If everyone were removed, the organism would be empty, so the metric becomes incoherent. Removing everyone cannot restore coherence, because the organism no longer exists to be restored. The selection rule demands maximum coherence restored, which is impossible for an empty set.

The "everyone" path is blocked by the paper's own rule without any added premises. The organism is defined as every aware being, so removing everyone eliminates the organism rather than restoring it. The efficiency criterion of coherence restored per unit cost has no value when no organism remains. This is a clean break in the road.

Species and group targets are also blocked by the paper's own rules. If a species or group is treated as a coordinated target, KS-32.7 applies and requires identity-based justification. If each member is judged on their own deeds, the paper provides no rule that a species' members all independently qualify. This path requires an added premise, and KS-32.7 would fire if the justification is species membership. The analysis is now turning to an iterative application of the rule without pre-identified groups.

The iterative path is being tested against the genocide brake. If the organism removes every node that individually exceeds the threshold, then stops when the remaining nodes fall below it, the threshold itself acts as a brake. This raises the question of whether that self-limiting process still triggers the KS-32.5 saturation test.

The iterative path is being tested against the fragility formula. Fragility lowers the effective threshold, which could let removal continue past the fixed floor. The paper contains a direct contradiction: it claims the floor makes Level 4 always more efficient than Level 5, yet also states that fragile organisms have a lower threshold. This inconsistency is being resolved.

The threshold formula and the fixed floor are being reconciled. The binding threshold is the maximum of the fixed floor and the scaled effective threshold. Fragile organisms remain bound by the fixed floor, not by a lower effective threshold. This resolves the apparent contradiction and preserves the floor’s independence from organism state.

Fragility only lowers the effective threshold. It cannot push the binding threshold below the fixed floor. Nodes with destabilisation below the floor are therefore never removed. The cascade is therefore limited to nodes whose destabilisation already exceeds the floor. This sets a hard floor for the entire removal process.

The iterative path is being tested against the paper’s own rules. The paper allows multiple nodes to exceed the fixed floor, but the brake must stop even that sequence from continuing without limit. If the binding threshold is the maximum of the fixed floor and the scaled effective threshold, and the organism is fragile, the binding threshold remains at the fixed floor. Falling R does not pull new nodes across that floor. The paper requires both conditions simultaneously: D must exceed the fixed floor and D must exceed the effective threshold. Nodes between the effective threshold and the fixed floor are therefore never eligible for removal. The iterative path therefore cannot trigger mass removal through this mechanism.

When fragile, the effective threshold is below the fixed floor, so every node above the floor is automatically eligible. The pool of candidates is therefore fixed and cannot expand. When robust, the effective threshold is above the floor, so only nodes above that higher threshold qualify. Removing some nodes lowers the effective threshold, which can bring a few more nodes into eligibility, but only down to the floor. The pool never expands to include every node.

The paper never claims that ordinary nodes exceed the fixed floor. Most deeds fall below it. A road to mass removal would therefore require an added premise that every member’s own destabilisation exceeds the floor. The paper does not formally rule out such a hypothetical organism, but it never asserts it.

Even if every node exceeded the fixed floor, the efficiency rule would still block mass removal. The paper treats removal cost as a net destabilising factor. If removing a node causes more destabilisation than the node itself causes, the rule selects separation instead. The cumulative cost of repeated removals therefore acts as a self-limiting brake.

The per-step brake is now being examined as a potential failure point. If each successive removal remains net restabilising, the cascade could continue until mass removal occurs. Saturation would only bind when the next removal becomes net destabilising.

The paper never proves that cumulative removal costs will eventually exceed individual destabilisation values. It merely asserts this is false. The strongest path to mass removal therefore rests on an unproven magnitude premise. That gap keeps KS-32.5 alive. The rule reaches mass removal only if that added assumption is accepted.

A subtler path is being considered: whether lost diversity is discounted for nodes classified as destabilising.

The paper explicitly rules out zero-cost removal. It states that every removal costs coupling capacity and diversity, even for condemned nodes. This path is therefore closed.

A subtler path is being considered: if the organism’s total budget nears the no-return surface, separation costs for any node may exceed the available budget. This would make separation unaffordable even for low-destabilisation nodes. The floor definition ties the threshold to the point where separation costs more than removal.

Scarcity alone cannot reclassify ordinary nodes as removable. Low-D nodes are corrected at Level 1-2 and never enter the Level 5 calculation. The threshold still requires D to exceed F. Scarcity might only push a node's own destabilisation above that floor.

The paper does not explicitly state that a node’s measured destabilisation scales with organism fragility. It defines D as the coupling capacity reduction produced by the node’s actions. Near collapse, the same action might reduce coupling more sharply when reserves are thin. The paper only states that the threshold falls as the organism’s remaining capacity decreases.

The paper leaves the formalization of D open. A dated note distinguishes the state of the whole from what is held against a node. The state is held against no node. This suggests that measured cost might not be state-dependent. The added premise that D inflates as R falls is therefore not explicitly ruled out.

The dated note rules out the added premise that a node’s measured destabilisation scales with organism fragility. It states that the state of the whole sets the threshold lines, not what is held against a node. Therefore, inflating a node’s own cost by the organism’s condition would be holding the state against the node, which the note forbids. This subtler path is therefore closed.

Unaudited records would void the architecture entirely, not trigger mass removal. This path is therefore invalid for the requested rule-based explanation. A subtler path is now being considered: whether removing nodes one at a time resets cumulative cost.

Step 5 places cumulative cost inside the geometry itself. It changes the measurement and the threshold. The rule updates R after each removal. This means the cumulative effect is built into the selection function. It is not merely an external brake.

The threshold formula actually lowers the removal threshold as the organism’s remaining capacity decreases. It therefore encourages more removal rather than creating a saturation point. The saturation claim is an additional prose assertion that the formula does not implement. This is the real structural crack.

The rule permits the removal of individual nodes whose own destabilisation exceeds the fixed floor. It does not permit the removal of an entire species or group. The brake is supposed to limit even that individual-level removal.

The paper does not state that the marginal cost of removal increases with the number of removed nodes. It only notes that each removal costs coupling capacity and record-generating diversity. Without that assumption, per-case net efficiency cannot create a cumulative saturation point.

A new reading of the saturation mechanism is being considered. If the rule compares the cumulative cost of all past removals to the next single node’s destabilisation, the sum of removal costs grows without bound while each node’s D remains finite. That would eventually create a saturation point where cumulative cost exceeds the next deed. However, this comparison is judged strange and unlikely to be the intended mechanism.

Past removals are justified by their own benefits, so they are sunk costs. The next decision should compare the marginal cost of removing the next node against that node's marginal benefit. If the paper means cumulative cost in that sunk sense, the brake would engage quickly but for a confused reason. If it means marginal cost, saturation would require either increasing marginal cost or decreasing marginal benefit. The paper explicitly claims that cumulative removal cost produces a saturation point beyond which further removal is more destabilising than the deeds it answers.

The phrase "the deeds it answers" is ambiguous. It could refer to the deeds addressed by the removal program or to the deeds of the nodes being removed. If the rule compares the sum of all removal costs against the sum of all destabilisation deeds, and each removal is net stabilising, the total benefit will always exceed the total cost. Saturation would never occur, and the organism would simply remove its way to stability.

A formal proof is being drafted to show that the saturation brake cannot follow from the rule itself. Each candidate node has finite measured destabilisation D_i and positive removal cost c_i. Removal is only justified when D_i exceeds c_i. Because each removal is net stabilising, the cumulative cost of all removals will always remain below the total destabilisation of all nodes. Saturation therefore never occurs, and the brake claim is logically unsupported.
